reading.title: reading-shell with defaults
reading.code:
{{-- The CSS variable on the shell wrapper cascades to the inner spine so it renders narrow enough to fit alongside the article in this iframe; the article below reserves matching padding-right. --}}

Introduction

The shell renders a progress bar, a sidebar TOC, and a bookmark prompt with sensible defaults — drop your article body inside, pass a bookmark key, and the rest is opinionated defaults. The progress bar pins to the very top of this iframe; the spine sits at the right edge; the bookmark arms itself once you've dwelled long enough.

Scroll this preview to see all three primitives respond. The bar fills, the spine highlights the active heading, and after 30 seconds of dwell, the bookmark prompt appears bottom-right (only on a return visit — first visit shows nothing).

The shell wrapper is the 80% case: pass a bookmark key, accept the comfortable density default. For finer control, decompose into primitives and mount each one directly.

Body

Each primitive in the family carries its own Alpine state; nothing communicates between them. That makes the composition robust to changes in any one of them — opt out per-toggle (:spine="false") or pick a density preset (density="compact") without breaking the others.

The four primitives the shell composes by default: reading-progress (the bar), reading-spine (the sidebar TOC), reading-bookmark (the dwell-triggered prompt), reading-meta (time-to-read estimate, off by default). The minimap and TOC primitives are toggleable but disabled in the comfortable density preset — opt in via :minimap="true" / :toc="true".

The density preset (comfortable, compact, minimal) flips per-primitive defaults. compact uses a thinner progress bar and forces the spine to always-md expanded. minimal shows only the progress bar.

Conclusion

For per-primitive customization beyond what toggles + density cover, compose primitives directly. The shell covers the common case; dropping to primitives covers the rest, with no "shell-with-overrides" half-step in between.

The shell's div wrapper is the only structural element it adds. If your layout needs the article body to live inside a flex/grid container or a Livewire boundary, the shell's wrapper might interfere — that's the canonical signal to drop the shell and mount primitives directly.

Click any spine link to smooth-scroll to that heading. Click anywhere else to return reading. The bookmark saves your offset every second; on a real return visit (after 30s+ dwell time), it'll prompt you to resume.

reading.title: Bar (default)
reading.code:
Watch the bar fill as the page scrolls

The reading-progress bar pins to the very top of the iframe (its position: fixed anchors to the iframe's viewport, not the outer page). Scroll inside this preview frame — the bar's fill grows from 0% to 100% as the scroll position moves from 0 to the bottom.

The fill animation uses transform: scaleX — a compositor-only property, so the bar fills smoothly even on low-powered devices without triggering layout or paint. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce the transition collapses to 0.01ms; the value still updates on scroll, only the interpolation is removed.

Default height is 3px (height="md"). Pass height="sm" for a 2px hairline or height="lg" for a 5px chunky bar. The color is the accent token by default; pass variant="success" / variant="warning" / variant="danger" for semantic states.

The bar starts hidden until the reader has scrolled past showAfter pixels (default 0). Set a higher value (e.g. :showAfter="100") if you want the bar to appear only after the reader has committed to reading past the article header.

Pass :milestones="true" to fire wirekit:reading-progress:milestone events at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. Useful for analytics or for triggering a "you're halfway through" prompt where it makes sense.

The progress bar lives in its own DOM node and never interferes with the document flow — even when nested inside other components, it takes itself out of layout via position: fixed the moment it mounts.

If your page has a fixed header above the article, set position="bottom" to pin the bar to the viewport bottom instead. Both positions share the same Alpine state machine; only the rendered DOM differs.

For embedded contexts like browser extensions or iframes-within-iframes where the bar should match surrounding text color, pass variant="auto". The fill resolves to currentColor, so the bar inherits whatever color the surrounding context provides.

Keep scrolling — the more text you scroll past, the more visible the bar's fill becomes. By the end of this preview block the bar should be at or near 100%.

The progress bar is the lightest of the reading-* primitives — pure CSS plus a single rAF-throttled scroll listener. No IntersectionObserver, no localStorage, no DOM scanning of headings.

reading.title: Dot indicator
reading.code:
Watch the dot fill as the page scrolls

Scroll inside this preview frame and the dot's stroke fills clockwise as the scroll position progresses from 0 to the bottom. Same Alpine state machine as the bar variant; only the rendered DOM differs. The dot pins to the bottom-right of the iframe via position: fixed and renders as a circular SVG with a stroke that fills as the reader progresses.

The fill animation uses stroke-dasharray on the SVG circle — also a compositor-only property, GPU-accelerated. The dot doesn't take itself out of layout (it sits in its own fixed-position container), so it never interferes with the article flow below.

Use the dot variant when a horizontal bar would interfere with your layout — for example, if you already have a fixed top nav or a persistent CTA at the top. The dot is also less visually heavy than the bar; some product surfaces want the indicator to be discoverable but not prominent.

Hover the dot to see the percentage tooltip (the percentage is also exposed via the dot's aria-label for screen readers). On touch, the tooltip is suppressed; the percentage is still available via assistive tech.

Pass position="bottom-left" / position="top-left" / position="top-right" to relocate the dot. The default bottom-right follows the convention every messaging app and chat surface uses for "your status indicator".

The dot variant carries the same variant prop as the bar (primary, neutral, success, warning, danger, info, auto) — the color token threading is identical.

Both indicators (bar and dot) ship a @media print { display: none !important } rule via the .wk-reading-progress marker class. Print-friendly; the article body prints clean without progress chrome on every page.

If you need both indicators simultaneously (a bar for "where am I" plus a dot for ambient feedback), mount two <x-wirekit::reading-progress> tags side by side. Both share scroll state via the same plugin; neither knows about the other.

Keep scrolling to see the dot fill. The stroke completes as the reader hits the bottom of the article.

toolbar.title: Sticky toolbar pinned at top of scrollable container
toolbar.code:
Save Discard

Scroll this panel — the toolbar above stays pinned to the top while the body below scrolls. The sticky-pin uses native CSS position: sticky against the nearest scrolling ancestor (this overflow:auto wrapper), so no JS scroll listener is needed and the behavior holds at any viewport.

For the sticky to work the toolbar's parent must be either a scrolling container (this wrapper) or the document root. Mounting a sticky toolbar inside a parent with overflow: hidden or a flex layout that constrains height will pin it against the wrong ancestor — opt out by setting :sticky="false" when the toolbar lives inside a non-scrolling card.

Filler content to demonstrate the scroll. Each paragraph adds vertical real estate that pushes the bottom of the panel beyond the visible viewport. The toolbar tracks the top boundary as the reader scrolls.

Use sticky toolbars for primary actions in long-form admin panels (Save / Discard for an edit screen, Filter / Sort for a long results list, Compose / Reply for a mail thread). Avoid for read-only contexts where the toolbar's affordances are unrelated to the body content.

Combine with density="compact" to minimize the height the sticky toolbar reserves at the top of the scrollable region — useful when vertical space is tight.

The sticky pin respects the container's top offset, so if the scrolling ancestor itself has padding-top, the toolbar pins below the padding rather than against the raw scroll edge.

More filler. The sticky should now be visibly anchored. Scroll back to the top to see the toolbar return to its document-flow position; the pinning is purely a scroll-position behavior, not a layout shift.

End of the scrollable body. The toolbar above is the last thing you see at the top regardless of how far down you scroll.
